summary: A 1970 note discussing a possible protocol plateau, a point at which the protocols might be considered stable enough to build on. It is a discussion piece by Jon Postel and Steve Crocker.

eli5.summary: Imagine climbing a hill and finding a flat spot to rest. This note asks if the rules could settle into a stable place.

questions: what is the network control program
how should the ncp handle errors
subtitle: Settling on core protocol design choices for the early network.

tldr.problem: As the ARPA network grows, many design questions emerge about how the Network Control Program should work: how to handle message padding, whether to support reconnection, how to report errors, and many others.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 48 by Postel and Crocker reviews each issue, explains the trade-offs, and proposes recommendations for a stable baseline protocol.
tldr.outcome: Several key decisions shaped the NCP protocol, including support for dynamic reconnection, error logging, status queries, and reserved link numbers for experimentation.

today: RFC 48 is not Internet Standard but captures important early protocol thinking. Many of its recommendations were adopted or influenced later NCP and TCP/IP designs, such as reserved port ranges for experimentation and the principle of layered protocol design.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
By April 1970, network researchers at UCLA and BBN (Bolt, Beranek and Newman) had proposed many ideas for improving the early NCP protocol. Jon Postel and Steve Crocker of UCLA collected these suggestions and analyzed each one, deciding which to adopt, which to defer, and which to reject.

This RFC presents their analysis and policy recommendations on ten major topics, plus a brief sketch of the NCP's internal structure. While not every suggestion was adopted, the document influenced protocol design for years.
sections.eli5: The designers got lots of suggestions and had to decide which ideas made sense and which didn't.

sections.title: Key Design Decisions
sections.content:
The RFC covers major questions including message padding alignment, whether to support dynamic reconnection of messages to different sockets, how to decouple links from connections, error reporting mechanisms, and status testing commands. On padding, the authors recommend using marking (a special bit string) rather than double padding to align messages to word boundaries.

On reconnection, they initially rejected it as complex, but later adopted a simpler scheme where login uses well-known sockets. They recommend error generation be optional and errors be logged locally rather than bombarded back to the sender. They propose link 255 be reserved for status and echo commands for debugging.
sections.eli5: Should messages be padded one way or another? Should you be able to switch a connection to a different receiver mid-stream? The designers work through the pluses and minuses of each choice.

sections.title: Protocol Layers
sections.content:
The authors identify three protocol layers: the IMP (Interface Message Processor) network layer, the NCP (Network Control Program) at the host level, and the user or subsystem level above. They emphasize keeping the NCP layer simple and neutral, leaving application-specific behavior to the user level.

They reserve link numbers 2 through 31 for regular connections, leaving 32 to 255 for experimentation. Control command prefixes from 255 downward are also reserved for experimental features, allowing researchers to try new ideas without disrupting the standard protocol.
sections.eli5: Networks work in layers: the IMP carries packets, the NCP manages connections, and applications do their own thing. Keep the middle layer simple and leave a corner for trying new things.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The authors stress that their proposed protocol is an implementation suggestion, not a requirement. Each site can vary the design to meet its needs. System calls, data structures and process models are illustrative only and should be adapted to each operating system.

The RFC represents an important moment in protocol design: a freeze-frame on architectural decisions that let the network grow from a handful of machines to a functioning system. The balance between simplicity and capability set precedents that influenced internet protocols for decades.
sections.eli5: This is a snapshot of what the designers thought would work. Every site can implement it their own way, as long as the messages on the wire match the spec.
